The billion-dollar mistake

In 1965, Tony Hoare — a computer scientist later knighted for his contributions, and the inventor of the quicksort algorithm — added a null reference to the type system of ALGOL W, a language he was designing. The idea was simple and appealing: every reference type gets one extra value meaning "points at nothing," so you don't need a separate mechanism for optional values.

In a talk in 2009, he called it his "billion-dollar mistake", and the reasoning is worth understanding rather than just quoting. The problem isn't that "nothing" needs representing — programs genuinely need to express absence. The problem is that null was made a member of every reference type, which means the type system stops being able to distinguish "a string" from "a string, or nothing." Every single value becomes potentially absent, the compiler can no longer help you tell the difference, and so the check has to happen in the programmer's head at every single use site, forever. Hoare's estimate of the cost — in crashes, vulnerabilities and damage across decades — was a billion dollars, and he was probably being conservative.

Nearly every mainstream language of the following forty years repeated the mistake: Java, C#, Python, PHP, JavaScript. The languages that didn't — ML, Haskell, and later Rust, Swift and Kotlin — did the same thing instead: they made absence an explicit, separate type (Option, Maybe, ?), so that a value which might be missing is visibly a different type from one that can't be, and the compiler forces you to deal with the difference.

Why TypeScript shipped with the hole open

TypeScript 0.8 through 1.x had exactly the same problem as JavaScript, deliberately. null and undefined were assignable to every type — a string could be null, a User could be undefined, and the compiler said nothing.

This was not an oversight. Return to the adoption constraint from Node 0: TypeScript had to accept enormous quantities of existing JavaScript with minimal friction. In real JavaScript, values are nullish constantly — DOM queries return null when nothing matches, array searches return undefined when nothing is found, optional configuration properties are simply absent. A TypeScript that rejected all of that on day one would have produced thousands of errors on the first file of any real project, and the tool would have been abandoned before anyone experienced its benefits. So the hole stayed open, and the most valuable check the language could offer was left switched off.

TypeScript 2.0, in September 2016, added strictNullChecks as an opt-in flag. This is, in my view and fairly widely, the most valuable single feature the language has ever shipped — it converts the largest class of production runtime crashes into compile errors. And it arrived four years after the language did, behind a flag, because the migration cost was understood to be enormous. That sequencing tells you something true about the whole ecosystem: the most valuable safety feature in TypeScript is one that a great many existing codebases still have switched off, because turning it on is a project rather than a setting.

Why the flags multiplied

Once one opt-in strictness flag existed, the pattern was established: add new checks as flags so existing code keeps compiling, let teams adopt them when they can afford to. That's how noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis and useUnknownInCatchVariables accumulated — each solving a specific unsoundness, each too disruptive to impose retroactively.

The strict umbrella flag exists because the individual list became unmemorable and because new strictness flags keep being added. Setting strict: true opts into the family and into future additions, which is the correct default for a new project and a decision to weigh carefully in an old one.

The mechanism, traced

What actually changes

Without strictNullChecks:

let name: string = null;      // fine
let user: User = undefined;   // fine
function greet(u: User) {
  return u.name.toUpperCase(); // fine — and crashes if u is null
}

Every type silently contains two extra values. The compiler cannot help you, because it has no way to express the difference between a value that might be absent and one that can't be.

With strictNullChecks on, null and undefined become their own types, assignable only where declared:

let name: string = null;
// error: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'string'.

let name2: string | null = null;   // fine — you said so

And now something important connects back: string | null is just a union (Node 4). Nothing new was invented. The rule that "a union only permits operations valid for every member" applies unchanged — so name2.toUpperCase() is an error, because null has no .toUpperCase(), and the fix is ordinary narrowing:

if (name2 !== null) {
  name2.toUpperCase(); // narrowed to string
}

This is why Node 4 had to come first. strictNullChecks doesn't add a null-checking feature — it removes an exemption, and lets the union machinery you already have do the work. Every technique from the previous node applies: early returns narrow the rest of the function, truthiness checks narrow (with a caveat below), and narrowing on a mutable object property is discarded after a function call.

One subtlety with truthiness narrowing worth flagging now, because it's a real bug source: if (value) excludes null and undefined, but also excludes 0, "", NaN and false. For a string | null, if (str) treats the empty string as absent — which is sometimes what you want and sometimes silently wrong. if (str !== null) or if (str != null) says precisely what you mean. That second form, with the loose !=, is the one idiomatic use of loose equality in TypeScript: x != null is a compact, well-understood check for "neither null nor undefined," and the compiler narrows correctly on it.

The optional property connection

Node 3 introduced optional properties. Under strictNullChecks their meaning becomes precise:

interface Options { timeout?: number }

function run(o: Options) {
  o.timeout.toFixed(); // error: 'o.timeout' is possibly 'undefined'
}

timeout?: number means the property's type is number | undefined. It's a union, and you narrow it. Without strict null checks the ? was decorative — the compiler let you read it as a plain number regardless.

The ergonomics: ?. and ??

These two operators are what make strict null checking livable rather than exhausting. Both are JavaScript, standardised in ES2020, and both are understood precisely by the type checker.

Optional chaining short-circuits an entire access chain:

const city = user?.address?.city;   // string | undefined

If user is nullish, evaluation stops immediately and the whole expression is undefined — address is never touched, so no crash. Crucially, the result type includes undefined, so the compiler still makes you handle the absence. It removes the tedium of nested checks without removing the obligation.

It also works for calls and index access: fn?.() calls only if fn isn't nullish; arr?.[0] indexes only if arr isn't nullish.

Nullish coalescing supplies a default:

const timeout = options.timeout ?? 5000;   // number

Now the reason it exists rather than just using ||, which is a genuinely common bug and a frequent interview question:

const retries = options.retries || 3;   // 0 becomes 3 — wrong
const retries2 = options.retries ?? 3;  // 0 stays 0 — right

|| fires on any falsy value, so a legitimate 0, an intentional empty string, or an explicit false all get silently replaced by the default. ?? fires only on null and undefined. Any time the value's type includes a meaningful falsy value — a count, a threshold, a flag, a name that might legitimately be empty — || is a bug waiting for the right input. The two operators combine naturally: const city = user?.address?.city ?? "unknown".

The rest of the strict family

strict: true enables all of these. Each is worth knowing by name, because you'll see them individually in real configs:

noImplicitAny — errors when the compiler can't infer a type and would otherwise fall back to any. Most commonly on function parameters, which have nothing to infer from (Node 1). This is second only to strictNullChecks in value, for a reason that connects forward to Node 9: an implicit any is the compiler silently inserting the one construct that disables checking, and it spreads from there.

strictFunctionTypes — makes function-type parameters checked contravariantly rather than bivariantly. This is Node 6's subject entirely; what matters here is that it only fixes the function-property syntax and deliberately leaves method syntax unsound.

strictBindCallApply — type-checks the arguments passed through .bind(), .call() and .apply(), which were previously typed loosely because expressing them properly required type-level machinery TypeScript didn't have until later.

strictPropertyInitialization — a class field declared name: string must actually be assigned, either at the declaration or in the constructor. Otherwise it's undefined at runtime while the type says string. Requires strictNullChecks to be on, since without it undefined is a legal string anyway. The escape hatches are name?: string (honest — it might be missing) or name!: string (the definite assignment assertion — "something else assigns this, trust me," carrying the same risk as any assertion).

noImplicitThis — errors when this inside a function has an inferred type of any, which happens in standalone functions where the call site determines this (Node 6).

useUnknownInCatchVariables — added in TypeScript 4.4, makes the variable in catch (e) typed unknown rather than any. This is correct and worth understanding rather than working around: JavaScript's throw can throw any value — a string, a number, a plain object, undefined. Nothing guarantees a thrown value is an Error. Code that reaches straight for e.message on an any is how error handlers throw their own errors while handling an error, producing a stack trace that points at your logging code instead of at the actual failure.

alwaysStrict — emits JavaScript's own "use strict" directive. Unrelated to type strictness; it's about the runtime language mode, and it's in the family for historical reasons.

The flag outside the family: noUncheckedIndexedAccess

const arr: string[] = [];
const first = arr[0];       // typed 'string' by default
first.toUpperCase();        // compiles — crashes at runtime

The default typing here is straightforwardly a lie: indexing an array can produce undefined, because the index can be out of range and because JavaScript arrays can have holes. noUncheckedIndexedAccess fixes it by typing every indexed read as T | undefined, which is correct.

It's outside strict because the friction is substantial — every array access, every dictionary lookup, every for loop over indices now needs handling, including the many cases where you can see by inspection that the index is valid and the compiler can't. It's a genuine judgement call rather than an obvious win, and the honest position in an interview is exactly that: correct, worth it in new code, an expensive retrofit in old code, and reasonable people disagree.

Related and also outside strict: exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which distinguishes a property that is absent from one explicitly set to undefined. Without it, { timeout: undefined } satisfies { timeout?: number }. With it, it doesn't — because "I didn't provide this" and "I explicitly provided nothing" are different statements, and code that branches on in or spreads objects can tell the difference. Also correct, also frictional.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Everything above means the same source file can compile cleanly in one repository and produce forty errors in another. tsconfig.json isn't a settings file in the sense that an editor's preferences are — it defines the dialect of TypeScript this repository speaks, and code is only meaningful relative to it. That's why the first file to read in an unfamiliar TypeScript codebase is its tsconfig, and why "does this compile?" is an incomplete question. Node 13 covers the file in full; this node is where you learn why it matters so much.

Turning it on, in practice

Since you'll do this to real code and the spec has you do it in recast Stage 1, the honest process:

Flip strict: true in a branch first, purely to measure. Count the errors by category — the compiler's error codes make this greppable — and expect noImplicitAny and strictNullChecks to account for the overwhelming majority.

Fix implicit any first, because it unblocks everything else: a parameter typed any means the compiler couldn't reason about anything downstream of it, so annotating it often resolves a cluster of unrelated-looking errors at once.

Then handle null errors by module rather than by error list, because they cluster around specific boundaries — the code that reads from the DOM, the code that parses input — and fixing one boundary properly resolves many downstream complaints.

And treat every ! you add as debt, not a fix. Each one is a place you turned off the check you just enabled. A small number are legitimate; a hundred means you've performed the migration without gaining anything from it.

In your project

Stage 1 of recast flips strict on as a single change, deliberately, to see the full blast radius at once — and the domain makes this an unusually good place to feel it. Browser file APIs are full of legitimately nullish values: FileReader.result can be null, canvas.getContext("2d") returns null when the browser can't allocate a context (which really happens for very large canvases), Blob operations can produce null on failure. Every one of those errors is the compiler being correct, not pedantic, and the spec asks you to resist the ! on enough of them to feel the difference between "I can prove this structurally" and "I don't want to deal with this right now."

Stage 6's environment parsing is this node meeting Node 15: process.env.REDIS_URL is typed string | undefined — correctly, since nothing guarantees it's set — and the wrong response is process.env.REDIS_URL!, which produces a server that starts fine and fails hours later with a cryptic connection error. The right response is parsing the whole environment through a schema at boot, so the process refuses to start with a legible message.

Stage 10 plants a ! on a canvas context that genuinely is null on the failing path, and separately turns on noUncheckedIndexedAccess to pay its cost across the codebase and decide honestly whether to keep it. Both are deliberately this node's material, planted so you experience the failure on your own code rather than someone else's.

In qbank

Worth checking directly rather than assuming: whether qbank's tsconfig.json has strict on at all, and if it does, whether the codebase is full of ! assertions that quietly undo it. Both are common in vibe-coded projects, because the fastest way past a strict-mode error is an assertion, and nothing later forces a reckoning.

If strict is off, that's the single highest-value change you could make to that codebase, and the fact that you'd now know how to stage the migration — measure, fix implicit any first, then boundaries by module — is exactly the kind of thing worth being able to describe in an interview about a project you own.

What an interviewer does with this

"What does strict do, and would you turn it on?" — extremely common. Strong answer names the family rather than just saying "makes it stricter," identifies strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny as the two that carry most of the value, and says yes for new projects while acknowledging the migration cost for existing ones.

"What's the difference between ?? and ||?" — a small question that reliably separates people who have shipped from people who have read. ?? only fires on nullish; || fires on any falsy value, so a legitimate 0 or empty string gets silently replaced. Having a concrete bug story — a retry count of 0 becoming 3 — is better than the definition alone.

"How would you migrate a large codebase to strictNullChecks?" — a genuinely senior question, because it's about staging risky change rather than about syntax. Not one commit; measure the blast radius first; implicit any first because it unblocks inference; then module by module at the boundaries; and treat added ! assertions as debt to revisit rather than as completion.

"Why is a caught error unknown?" — because JavaScript can throw anything, not just an Error. Reaching for e.message without narrowing is how an error handler throws its own error. The answer connects forward to Node 9 and shows you understand that the flag is correcting a real unsoundness rather than being awkward.

"Explain the null reference problem to someone who hasn't hit it." — occasionally asked as a communication test. Hoare's billion-dollar mistake, and the precise reason it's a mistake: making null a member of every type destroys the type system's ability to distinguish "a value" from "a value or nothing," so the check moves into the programmer's head at every use site forever.

sections.title: Node 6 — Functions and variance
sections.content:
Where this sits

Nodes 3 through 5 typed data — shapes, alternatives, absence. This node types the things that transform data, which is most of what you actually write. It also contains the single most misunderstood rule in the language: functions are compatible in two directions at once, and one of those directions runs opposite to everyone's intuition. Getting it wrong is how unsound code passes the checker, which is why it's a reliable senior-interview probe.

Every term, from absolute zero

Function type — a description of what a function accepts and returns, written with an arrow: (a: number, b: number) => number. It says nothing about the function's name or body — only its interface.

Signature — the parameter list and return type together. Two functions with the same signature are interchangeable as far as the type system is concerned (structural typing again, Node 2).

Parameter — a name in the function's declaration. Argument — the actual value passed at a call site. The distinction matters when discussing variance, so it's worth keeping straight: parameters are what a function promises to accept; arguments are what callers actually supply.

Callback — a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later. arr.map(x => x * 2) passes a callback.

Higher-order function — one that takes or returns functions. map, filter, and any middleware system are higher-order.

Substitutability — whether one thing can be used in place of another without breaking anything. The whole of this node is about when one function is substitutable for another.

Variance — how the substitutability of a compound type relates to the substitutability of its parts. If Dog is usable as Animal, is Array<Dog> usable as Array<Animal>? Is (x: Dog) => void usable as (x: Animal) => void? Variance is the name of the rules answering those questions. The word comes from mathematics, where it describes how something changes with respect to something else.

Covariant — varies in the same direction. If Dog is assignable to Animal, and Box<Dog> is assignable to Box<Animal>, then Box is covariant in its parameter. "Co-" as in "together."

Contravariant — varies in the opposite direction. If Dog is assignable to Animal, but Handler<Animal> is assignable to Handler<Dog> (note the flip), then Handler is contravariant. "Contra-" as in "against."

Bivariant — accepted in both directions, which is convenient and unsound. Neither co- nor contra-, but both.

Invariant — accepted in neither direction; the types must match exactly.

Sound / unsound — defined at Node 2: a sound rule never accepts a program that will fail at runtime. Bivariance is unsound, deliberately.

Contextual typing — introduced at Node 1, defined fully here: when a function is written in a position whose expected type is already known, its parameters take their types from that context rather than needing annotations.

Overload — several call signatures declared for one function, so it can be called in genuinely different ways with different result types.

Implementation signature — the single real signature underneath a set of overloads. It must be compatible with all of them and is not itself callable from outside.

this — a JavaScript keyword whose value is determined by how a function is called, not where it's defined. A deep JavaScript wart; TypeScript can only describe it, not fix it.

The history — why variance is a problem at all

Variance isn't a TypeScript invention; it's a problem every type system with generics or function types must solve, and the history is a series of languages getting it wrong in instructive ways.

Java, 1995, and array covariance. Java made arrays covariant: a String[] is usable as an Object[]. This was a deliberate decision made before Java had generics — without it, you couldn't write a single method that sorted arrays of anything, and the language would have been painfully limited. The consequence is a famous hole:

String[] strings = new String[1];
Object[] objects = strings;      // allowed — arrays are covariant
objects[0] = 42;                 // compiles fine
                                 // throws ArrayStoreException at runtime

Java's answer was to insert a runtime check on every array write, which costs performance forever and turns a type error into a crash rather than preventing it. The lesson the industry took: covariance is safe for reading and unsafe for writing, and mutable containers can't be covariant without a hole.

C#, 2005–2010. C# added generics without variance at first (invariant, safe, occasionally annoying), then added explicit in and out keywords in C# 4.0 so a library author could declare a type parameter contravariant or covariant deliberately. That's the "correct" design: variance is opt-in, per parameter, and checked. It also requires every library author to think about variance, which most don't want to do.

TypeScript's position. TypeScript infers variance structurally rather than requiring declarations, which fits the language's goal of describing existing JavaScript without asking anyone to annotate anything. And then it made one specific, deliberate, well-documented exception to soundness for method parameters — the bivariance hole — for reasons that are worth understanding rather than memorising, because they're the same reason you'll meet at every other hole in the language.

Here's the reason. Consider the DOM's addEventListener, or an array's sort, or any of hundreds of built-in APIs. The declaration for addEventListener accepts a listener taking a generic Event. But essentially all real code passes a listener typed for a specific event:

element.addEventListener("click", (e: MouseEvent) => {
  console.log(e.clientX);   // clientX only exists on MouseEvent
});

Under sound contravariance, this is an error — you're supplying a handler that requires MouseEvent where one accepting any Event is expected, and there's no guarantee the caller will only send mouse events. Sound rules would reject a pattern used in essentially every browser application ever written. So the rules bent. That's the whole story, and it's the same story as excess property checking, array covariance, and any: the sound version rejected too much working JavaScript, so TypeScript accepted a hole and documented it.

The mechanism, traced

Return types are covariant, and this is the intuitive direction

type GetAnimal = () => Animal;
type GetDog = () => Dog;   // Dog extends Animal

let f: GetAnimal;
const g: GetDog = () => new Dog();
f = g;   // allowed

Why this is safe, reasoned from the caller's position: whoever holds f expects to call it and receive an Animal. They get a Dog. A Dog is an Animal, so every operation they were entitled to perform still works. Nobody is surprised. Returning something more specific than promised is always safe.

The reverse fails, correctly:

let h: GetDog;
const i: GetAnimal = () => new Animal();
h = i;   // error

Someone holding h expects a Dog back and would call .bark() on it. They'd get a bare Animal that has no .bark(). Runtime crash. Rejected.

Parameters are contravariant, and this is the direction nobody guesses

type HandleAnimal = (a: Animal) => void;
type HandleDog = (d: Dog) => void;

let f: HandleDog;
const g: HandleAnimal = (a: Animal) => { console.log(a.name); };
f = g;   // allowed — the MORE GENERAL function is substitutable

Read that twice, because it's backwards from intuition. A function that accepts any animal can stand in for one that accepts only dogs. Reasoning it out from the caller's position again: whoever holds f believes they may pass a Dog to it. They pass a Dog. The actual function accepts any Animal, and a Dog is an Animal, so it handles it fine. It's simply more capable than required. Safe.

Now the unsafe direction, which is the one people expect to work:

let h: HandleAnimal;
const i: HandleDog = (d: Dog) => { d.bark(); };
h = i;   // unsound — should be an error

Whoever holds h believes they may pass any animal. They pass a Cat. The actual function immediately calls .bark() on it. Crash.

The general principle, worth stating in a sentence you can reproduce under pressure: a function is substitutable if it accepts at least as much and returns at most as much — more permissive in what it takes, more specific in what it gives.

There's a useful intuition for why the two directions differ, without any category theory: a function's parameters are things flowing in from the caller, and its return is a thing flowing out to the caller. Anything the function receives must be at least as broad as what callers might send; anything it emits must be at least as specific as what callers expect. Data flowing in and data flowing out have opposite safety requirements, so their variance is opposite.

The bivariance hole, precisely

Here is the exception, and it hinges on a syntactic distinction that looks meaningless and isn't:

interface Handlers {
  onEventMethod(e: Event): void;        // method syntax
  onEventProp: (e: Event) => void;      // property syntax
}

Those two members are checked by different rules. Method syntax is checked bivariantly — assignment is accepted in both directions, including the unsafe one. Property syntax is checked contravariantly if and only if strictFunctionTypes is on (Node 5), and bivariantly if it's off.

So under strict: true:

declare let handlers: Handlers;

handlers.onEventProp = (e: MouseEvent) => {};
// error: MouseEvent is not assignable to Event

handlers.onEventMethod = (e: MouseEvent) => {};
// allowed — bivariance, and genuinely unsound

Same shape of assignment. Same underlying risk. One errors, one doesn't, and the difference is which syntax was used to declare the member.

The reason for the exemption is the addEventListener story above, plus arrays. Array methods are declared with method syntax, and a great deal of code relies on passing narrower callbacks than the declaration technically allows. Making method parameters contravariant would have broken the standard library's usability for everyone, so the hole was left open specifically there.

Two practical consequences worth carrying. First: if you're declaring a callback member in an interface and you want the safe rule, use property syntax — onEvent: (e: Event) => void rather than onEvent(e: Event): void — and have strictFunctionTypes on. Second: know that this hole exists, because it's how an interviewer finds out whether you understand variance or have merely heard the words.

An honest caveat on strictFunctionTypes: it also only applies to function type positions, not to method declarations, and it doesn't apply to functions declared with the function keyword being assigned to interfaces in some legacy positions. The rule of thumb — method syntax is bivariant, property syntax under strict is contravariant — is accurate for almost everything you'll write.

Parameter count: why callbacks that ignore arguments work

[1, 2, 3].map((x) => x * 2);              // fine
[1, 2, 3].map((x, i, arr) => x * 2);      // also fine

map's callback is declared as taking three parameters — value, index, array — and passing one that takes only the first is accepted. A function with fewer parameters is assignable where one with more is expected.

This isn't a special case; it's the same substitutability reasoning. The caller will supply three arguments. Your function ignores two of them, which in JavaScript is entirely normal and completely harmless — extra arguments are simply unused. The reverse is rejected: a function requiring four parameters can't be used where only three will be supplied, because the fourth would be undefined while its type says otherwise.

This is also why ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) produces [1, NaN, NaN] — a classic JavaScript puzzle that TypeScript does not save you from, because parseInt legitimately takes two parameters and map legitimately supplies an index as the second, so the types line up perfectly while the semantics don't. Worth knowing as an honest example of what type checking cannot do for you.

Contextual typing, fully

const users = [{ name: "a" }, { name: "b" }];
users.map(u => u.name);       // u is inferred — no annotation needed

The parameter u needs no annotation because map's declaration says its callback takes an element of the array's type, and the compiler already knows what that is. The type flows into the function expression from its surrounding context. This is why idiomatic TypeScript has so few annotations on callbacks.

And the corollary that confuses everyone once:

const getName = u => u.name;
// error: Parameter 'u' implicitly has an 'any' type.
users.map(getName);

Extracted to a standalone const, the same function has no context to draw from. Nothing surrounds it that says what it will be called with. So inference has nothing to work with, and under noImplicitAny (Node 5) that's an error. The fix is either annotating it, or typing the whole constant as a function type so the parameter gets its type from that:

const getName: (u: { name: string }) => string = u => u.name;

Return type annotations: when to write them

The default should be inference, because an inferred return type stays honest as the body changes — you can't forget to update something you never wrote down (the same reasoning as Node 1's "annotate at the edges").

The exceptions are worth knowing precisely, because they're a senior-sounding detail that happens to be true:

Exported functions in a published package or across a package boundary. An explicit return type is a contract. Without it, an innocuous change to the body silently changes what your consumers see — and if that consumer is another team, you've made a breaking change without noticing. It also dramatically improves compile speed at scale, because the checker doesn't have to reconstruct a possibly-enormous inferred type at every call site, which is Node 18's material.

Recursive functions, where inference sometimes can't converge without help.

**Functions where you want the return type to be the *specification***, and the body to be checked against it — a function that must return a Result should say so, so that accidentally returning a bare value is an error rather than a silently widened return type.

Optional, default, and rest parameters

function f(a: number, b?: number, c = 0, ...rest: string[]) {}

b?: number has type number | undefined inside the body — it's optional at the call site and possibly absent inside, so you narrow it (Node 4).

c = 0 is optional at the call site but has type number inside — the default guarantees a value, so no narrowing is needed. This is usually what you want, and the distinction between ? and a default is worth being deliberate about.

...rest: string[] collects remaining arguments into an array. It must come last. With tuple types (Node 7), rest parameters can express a fixed head and variadic tail, which is how things like bind are typed.

Note that optional parameters must follow required ones — you cannot have f(a?: number, b: number), since there'd be no way to supply b without a.

Overloads, and why you should mostly avoid them

function parse(input: string): object;
function parse(input: string, asText: true): string;
function parse(input: string, asText?: boolean): object | string {
  // one implementation, handling both
}

The first two lines are call signatures — the shapes callers may use. The third is the implementation signature: it must be compatible with all the overloads, and it is not callable from outside. Callers see only the two declared overloads.

Overloads exist for genuinely different call shapes producing genuinely different result types. The reasons to avoid them where possible: the implementation signature is checked loosely against the overloads, so it's easy to declare an overload the implementation doesn't actually honour; they interact badly with generics; and in most cases a union parameter or a generic expresses the same relationship more clearly and with better inference. Modern TypeScript pushes toward generics and conditional types (Node 10) for what overloads used to do.

Typing this

JavaScript's this is determined by how a function is called, not where it's written — a fact that produces a whole family of bugs when a method is detached from its object and passed as a callback. TypeScript can't fix that, but it can describe it:

function handleClick(this: HTMLElement, e: Event) {
  console.log(this.tagName);
}

this here is a fake first parameter — it's erased entirely at compile time (Node 2) and exists only to state what the call site must provide. If you call the function in a way that doesn't supply that this, it's an error. noImplicitThis (Node 5) is what makes an untyped this in such a function an error rather than a silent any.

Arrow functions have no this of their own — they capture it from the enclosing scope — which is why arrow functions in class fields are the standard way to avoid the detached-method problem entirely.

In your project

Stage 3 of recast is where variance stops being theory. The converter registry holds a dozen converters with different input types, different options and different outputs, all sitting behind one dispatch function — and that's precisely the situation where parameter positions bite. The dispatcher accepts a general input; each converter accepts a specific one. Get the relationship backwards and you either can't compile at all or, worse, you compile and are unsound in exactly the way this node describes: a converter registered for JPEG being handed a HEIC because the type said it was fine.

The spec's warning that "converters have genuinely different failure modes, and unifying those without flattening them into useless strings takes a real design decision" is also a variance question underneath — the error type in a Result return is in return position, so it's covariant, and a union of specific error types is substitutable where a general one is expected. That falls out of the rules rather than needing a design meeting, once you know them.

Stage 5's worker message protocol is the other place: the handler for messages from a worker is a callback, and typing it as a property rather than a method (with strictFunctionTypes on) is what stops you from accidentally registering a handler that's narrower than the messages actually arriving.

And Stage 10 plants the bivariance failure deliberately — a converter typed too narrowly for the inputs it will receive, accepted by the compiler through method-syntax bivariance, failing at runtime. The spec notes it takes a few attempts to construct one that genuinely compiles, and that's a feature: the fiddliness is what makes the rule stick.

What an interviewer does with this

"Explain variance in TypeScript." — the flagship senior question for this node. A strong answer covers all four parts: returns are covariant (a more specific return is always safe); parameters are contravariant (a more general parameter is safe, which is the counterintuitive one); method parameters are bivariant, which is unsound; and strictFunctionTypes fixes only the function-property syntax. Being able to derive the safe direction from the caller's perspective, rather than reciting it, is what distinguishes a real answer.

"Is this assignment safe?" — followed by a handler being passed somewhere. The technique is always the same: ask what the caller is entitled to do, and check whether the substituted function honours that. Answering by reasoning rather than by rule-lookup is the signal.

"Why does TypeScript allow an obviously unsafe callback assignment?" — the bivariance question in disguise. The strong answer names the reason: sound contravariance would reject addEventListener with a MouseEvent handler, which is essentially every browser application ever written, so the rule was deliberately bent for method syntax. This is the same trade as excess property checking and array covariance — usability over soundness, documented as a non-goal.

"Why does extracting an arrow function into a variable cause an implicit-any error?" — checks whether contextual typing is understood as a mechanism rather than magic. Inline, the parameter's type came from the surrounding expression; standalone, there's nothing to infer from.

"Should exported functions have explicit return types?" — yes across a package or public boundary, because the annotation is the contract and prevents a body change from silently breaking consumers, and because it materially improves compile speed at scale. No internally, where inference stays honest as the code changes.

sections.title: Node 7 — Arrays, tuples, and as const
sections.content:
Where this sits

Nodes 3 through 6 typed single objects, alternatives, and functions. Almost everything real involves collections of those things, and JavaScript has one array type doing two genuinely different jobs — "many of the same kind of thing" and "a fixed sequence of specific things." This node gives each job its own type, and introduces the single small feature (as const) that will matter enormously once you reach type-level programming at Node 10.

Every term, from absolute zero

Array type — T[] or equivalently Array<T>, describing a list where every element is type T. The two spellings are identical to the compiler; pick one for consistency.

Homogeneous — every element the same type. number[] is homogeneous. (string | number)[] is a homogeneous array of a union — still one declared element type, just a broader one.

Tuple type — a fixed-length array where each position has its own specific type: [string, number] means exactly two elements, a string then a number. Unlike a plain array type, position carries meaning.

Rest element (in a tuple) — a variable-length tail after some fixed positions: [string, ...number[]] means "a string, then any number of numbers."

Labelled tuple element — a name attached to a tuple position purely for readability in editor tooltips: [x: number, y: number]. Erased at compile time like everything else; it changes nothing about behaviour.

as const — an assertion applied to a literal that makes it maximally specific and deeply readonly, rather than letting it widen to its general type.

Indexed access (on a type) — reading a type "at" a key or position, written T[K]. On a tuple or array, indexing with number gives the union of all element types.

Covariance (on arrays) — introduced at Node 6 for functions; here applied to arrays. JavaScript arrays are covariant and mutable, which is an unsound combination inherited from the same trade-off Java made in 1995.

Evolving array — a TypeScript-specific inference behaviour for a let-declared empty array with no annotation: the compiler watches what you push into it and gradually infers the element type from actual usage.

The mechanism, traced

Arrays: the common case, and its two rough edges

Array typing is mostly unsurprising — T[] propagates through the standard methods, so .map, .filter, .reduce all infer correctly because TypeScript ships declarations for every one of them (Node 1). Two places it doesn't quite behave as you'd expect are worth knowing before you hit them blind.

.filter(Boolean) doesn't narrow out null. A common pattern for removing empty values:

const values: (string | null)[] = ["a", null, "b"];
const filtered = values.filter(Boolean);
// type is still (string | null)[], not string[]

The runtime behaviour is correct — null really is removed. The type doesn't reflect it, because Boolean is just a function reference to the compiler; it has no special knowledge that calling it as a predicate narrows anything. The fix is a real type predicate (fully defined at Node 9), which the compiler does understand as narrowing:

const filtered = values.filter((v): v is string => v != null);
// string[]

.reduce often needs its accumulator annotated. Inference for reduce derives the accumulator's type from the initial value you pass, and that value is frequently narrower than you intend:

const grouped = items.reduce((acc, item) => {
  acc[item.category] ??= [];
  acc[item.category].push(item);
  return acc;
}, {});
// acc inferred as {} — nothing can be assigned to it

An empty object literal infers as {}, the type with no known members, so trying to index into it fails. Annotate the initial value explicitly — {} as Record<string, Item[]> or a typed generic argument to reduce — and inference has something real to work from.

Tuples: fixed positions, fixed meaning

function useCounter(): [number, () => void] {
  let count = 0;
  return [count, () => { count++; }];
}
const [value, increment] = useCounter();

This is the shape behind React's useState and any function returning a small fixed bundle of unrelated values. Without a tuple, the return type would be a plain array — (number | (() => void))[] — and destructuring would give both value and increment the combined union type, losing the fact that position one is always the number and position two is always the function. A tuple preserves that positional meaning.

Rest elements extend this to a fixed head plus a variable tail: [string, ...number[]] types something like printf(format, ...args). Labels add nothing functional — [x: number, y: number] behaves identically to [number, number] — they exist purely so an editor's hover tooltip says x and y instead of 0 and 1.

Tuple-ness is a compile-time-only claim. At runtime a tuple is an ordinary JavaScript array, and nothing stops .push() from lengthening it — the type says length two, the runtime array can grow to three, and the mismatch is silent until something reads past where it expects the tuple to end. Declaring it readonly closes the specific hole of accidental mutation through the typed reference, though it doesn't prevent every route to the same array being mutated elsewhere.

as const: freezing a literal at its most specific

Recall from Node 1 that let widens literals and const doesn't — const mode = "dark" has type "dark", not string. as const extends that same idea to entire structures, not just single values:

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
// inferred: string[]

const colorsConst = ["red", "green", "blue"] as const;
// inferred: readonly ["red", "green", "blue"]

Without it, an array literal widens each element to its general type and the array itself is a mutable string[] — reasonable, because you might push anything into it later. as const says the opposite: this is exactly these three values, in this exact order, and nothing may be added, removed, or changed. The result is a readonly tuple of literal types, not a plain array.

The same applies to object literals — { mode: "dark" } as const gives mode the literal type "dark" rather than the widened string, and marks the whole object readonly.

Deriving a union from data you already have

This is where as const stops being a curiosity and becomes something you reach for constantly, because it solves a duplication problem cleanly:

const STATUSES = ["pending", "active", "cancelled"] as const;
type Status = typeof STATUSES[number];
// "pending" | "active" | "cancelled"

Read the right side carefully, because both pieces matter. typeof STATUSES lifts the value STATUSES into type space (Node 10 covers this operator fully) — giving the type readonly ["pending", "active", "cancelled"]. Indexing that tuple type with number — exactly the same indexed-access idea as reading an array's element type — gives the union of everything at every position, which for a tuple of literals is the union of those literals.

The payoff: you now have one array, at runtime, that both drives your logic (iterate it to build a dropdown, validate against it, loop over it) and produces the type. Without as const, you'd either maintain the array and a separate hand-written union that can drift apart, or give up the runtime list entirely and hardcode the values twice. This is the same single-source-of-truth principle the whole topic keeps returning to, arriving here in its simplest form.

Array covariance: the inherited hole

const dogs: Dog[] = [new Dog()];
const animals: Animal[] = dogs;   // allowed
animals.push(new Cat());          // compiles — and corrupts `dogs`

TypeScript allows treating Dog[] as Animal[], exactly the way Node 6 covered functions treating a more specific return as substitutable. But arrays are mutable, and pushing a Cat through the Animal[] view actually writes into the same underlying array that dogs still points at — so dogs now silently contains a Cat, despite its type promising only dogs. This is precisely the Java 1995 problem from Node 6's history: covariance is safe for reading, unsafe for writing, and TypeScript — like Java — accepted the hole rather than reject the very common, usually-harmless pattern of passing a more specific array where a general one is expected for read-only purposes.

ReadonlyArray<T> (or readonly T[]) removes the mutating methods from the type, which prevents the specific push above, though it doesn't retroactively make the underlying assignment sound — it just stops your code from being the one that exploits the hole.

In your project

Stage 3 of recast builds the converter registry as an as const object specifically so the Format union can be derived from its keys rather than maintained separately — add a format to the table and the type updates itself, which is this node's central technique applied to the project's actual data.

Stage 4's route resolution over that registry works with tuples directly: a resolved conversion route (HEIC → JPEG → PDF) is naturally a tuple of steps, and reading the route's length and specific positions at the type level is indexed access on a tuple, extended into recursion at Node 10.

Stage 9's .filter(Boolean) trap is exactly the kind of thing the spec expects you to hit once in the batch-conversion UI — filtering out failed jobs from a results list and discovering the type still claims failures might be present, until a real type predicate is written.

What an interviewer does with this

"What's the difference between an array type and a tuple type?" — a plain definitional question that's really testing whether you reach for tuples at all. Strong answer: array types are homogeneous and variable-length; tuples are fixed-length with a distinct type per position, and they're how you type things like useState's return without losing which value is which.

"How would you derive a union type from a list of allowed values without maintaining both by hand?" — this is specifically testing as const plus indexed access. const arr = [...] as const; type T = typeof arr[number] is the expected answer, and being able to explain why the plain array widens without as const shows real understanding rather than a memorised snippet.

"Why doesn't .filter(Boolean) remove null from the type?" — a small, concrete gotcha question. The compiler has no special knowledge that Boolean narrows; only an explicit type predicate does. Knowing the fix cold suggests you've actually hit this rather than only read about unions.

sections.title: Node 8 — Generics
sections.content:
Where this sits

Every node so far has typed things you knew the type of when you wrote the code. This node handles the case where you genuinely don't — where the same code is correct for many types and you need to say so without lying. It's the gateway to Node 10's type-level programming, and it's the node where recast's registry and SDK live.

Every term, from absolute zero

Generic — code parameterised by a type. The word comes from "generic programming," a term from the C++ and Ada traditions of the 1980s meaning "algorithms written once, usable for many types."

Type parameter — a placeholder for a type, declared in angle brackets: <T>. It behaves like a variable, except its values are types rather than data.

Type argument — the actual type supplied for a parameter at a use site. In Array<string>, string is the type argument.

T — conventional name for a type parameter, from "Type." Other conventions: K for a key, V for a value, E for an element or error, R for a return type. These are conventions only — nothing in the language treats them specially, and a descriptive name like TFormat is often better in a complex signature.

Instantiation — supplying type arguments to a generic, producing a concrete type. Array<string> is an instantiation of Array<T>.

Inference (of type arguments) — the compiler working out type arguments from the values you passed, so you don't have to write them.

Constraint — a restriction on what a type parameter may be, written with extends: <T extends { length: number }>. Note that extends here means assignable to — the structural relation from Node 2 — not class inheritance.

Inference site — a position in a signature where the compiler can learn a type parameter's value from an argument. A parameter typed T[] is an inference site for T.

Default type parameter — a fallback used when no type argument is supplied and none can be inferred: <T = string>.

const type parameter — <const T>, added in TypeScript 5.0, making inference behave as if the caller had written as const (Node 7).

NoInfer<T> — a utility added in TypeScript 5.4 that excludes a position from being used as an inference site, so a type parameter gets decided by the argument you intended rather than by an unrelated one.

Generic class / generic interface / generic type alias — the same parameterisation applied to those declarations rather than to a function.

Higher-kinded types — parameterising over a generic type itself rather than over a concrete type. TypeScript doesn't have them; mentioned only because it explains why some functional-programming patterns from Haskell or Scala can't be expressed cleanly here, and it's occasionally raised in interviews to see whether you know the limits.

The history — why generics exist at all

The problem generics solve predates TypeScript by decades and is easiest to see in the language that got it wrong most publicly.

Java before 2004 had no generics. A List held Object — the universal supertype — so putting a String in and getting one out required a cast on every read:

List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("devansh");
String n = (String) names.get(0);   // cast required, unchecked

That cast is a promise, not a check. Put an Integer in the same list and the cast throws ClassCastException at runtime — the exact class of error the type system was supposed to prevent, reintroduced at every single use site. The type system knew "this is a list of something" and the programmer knew "this is a list of strings," and there was no way to write the second fact down.

C++ templates (1990s) solved it differently, and understanding the difference matters for TypeScript. A C++ template generates a separate copy of the code for every type it's used with — vector<int> and vector<string> are genuinely different compiled functions. That's called monomorphisation, it's fast, and it's why C++ compile times and binary sizes are what they are.

Java 5, in 2004, added generics with erasure (the same word from Node 2): List<String> is checked at compile time and becomes plain List in the compiled output. One implementation, no code generation, backward compatible with pre-generics libraries. The cost is that Java cannot ask at runtime what a list contains, which is the well-known irritation of new T() being impossible there too.

C# 2.0, in 2005 — designed by Hejlsberg — did the opposite: reified generics, where type arguments survive into the runtime and can be inspected. It's more capable and it required deeper changes to the runtime.

So when Hejlsberg came to TypeScript, he had personally built both a reified generic system (C#) and knew the erased one (Java). TypeScript necessarily took the erased path, because reification would require runtime support and the entire design constraint from Node 2 was no runtime artefacts, no runtime library, output that looks like hand-written JavaScript. There is no possible TypeScript in which generics survive to runtime, because there is no TypeScript runtime for them to survive into.

This isn't a limitation to work around; it's the direct consequence of the constraint that made the language adoptable at all, and knowing the lineage lets you answer "why can't I do new T()?" with history rather than a shrug.

The mechanism, traced

The problem, concretely

Write a function returning the first element of an array. Three attempts, and only the third is right:

function first(arr: any[]): any {
  return arr[0];
}
const name = first(["a", "b"]);   // name: any — checking is now off downstream

any compiles and destroys the answer (Node 9 covers why it's contagious). The caller knew they had strings; the function threw that away.

function firstString(arr: string[]): string | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}

Correct, and useless for anything but strings. You'd need one of these per type, forever.

function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}

const name = first(["a", "b"]);      // string | undefined
const count = first([1, 2, 3]);      // number | undefined
const user = first(users);           // User | undefined

T is a placeholder filled in per call site. The function is written once, and the relationship between what goes in and what comes out is preserved rather than erased. That preservation is the entire point: any breaks the link between input and output, and a generic maintains it.

The mental model that makes this stop being intimidating, from the landscape: a generic is a function that takes types as arguments and returns a type. Array<T> takes a type and gives you back a type. first<T> takes a type and gives you back a function signature. Same idea as an ordinary function, one level up.

Inference: why you almost never write the type argument

You can write it explicitly — first<string>(["a"]) — and you almost never do, because the compiler infers it:

Here's the actual process for first(["a", "b"]). The compiler computes the argument's type: string[]. It matches that against the parameter's declared type, T[]. Structural matching gives T = string. It substitutes throughout the signature, producing (arr: string[]) => string | undefined for this call. Nothing clever is happening — it's pattern matching a type against a type shape and reading off the bindings.

Inference works from inference sites — positions where a type parameter appears in a parameter type. A parameter typed T or T[] or (x: T) => void all give the compiler something to match against. A type parameter appearing only in the return type has no inference site, so it can't be inferred and the caller must supply it (or it falls back to unknown, which is usually a sign the signature is wrong).

When multiple arguments mention the same parameter, the compiler collects candidates from each and picks a best common type — which is why passing a string and a number to <T>(a: T, b: T) infers T = string | number rather than erroring.

Constraints: making T usable

An unconstrained T means "literally any type," so you can do essentially nothing with it:

function longest<T>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length > b.length ? a : b;
  //       ~~~~~~ Property 'length' does not exist on type 'T'
}

Correct rejection — T could be number, which has no .length. A constraint restricts the parameter while still returning the caller's precise type:

function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length > b.length ? a : b;
}

const s = longest("hello", "hi");        // string
const arr = longest([1, 2], [1, 2, 3]);  // number[]

Both work because both have .length. The return type is still T, so s is a string, not the constraint type — which is the crucial difference from just typing the parameters as { length: number } and losing everything specific about them.

Say the extends thing out loud once more, because it genuinely trips people: it means "is assignable to," the structural relation from Node 2. T extends { length: number } doesn't mean T inherits from anything. It means any type whose shape includes a numeric length qualifies — strings, arrays, and any object you define with that member.

The canonical constrained generic

The pattern worth being able to write from memory, because it appears in every interview and in real code constantly:

function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

const user = { name: "devansh", age: 27 };
const n = get(user, "name");   // string
const a = get(user, "age");    // number
get(user, "email");            // error: not assignable to "name" | "age"

Two type parameters, linked. keyof T is the union of T's keys (Node 10 covers it properly) — here "name" | "age". K is constrained to be one of them, so a wrong key is a compile error with the valid options listed. And the return type T[K] is indexed access: the type of T at key K, computed per call site — string when K is "name", number when it's "age".

This is where generics stop feeling like ceremony. Three type-level pieces cooperating to make an ordinary property lookup fully safe, with no runtime cost and no annotations at the call site.

Generics everywhere else

Not just functions:

interface Box<T> { value: T }
type Pair<A, B> = [A, B];

class Cache<T> {
  private items = new Map<string, T>();
  get(key: string): T | undefined { return this.items.get(key); }
  set(key: string, value: T): void { this.items.set(key, value); }
}

And you have been using generic types all along without writing one: Array<T>, Promise<T>, Map<K, V>, Set<T>, Record<K, V>. Every one is a type parameterised by another type.

Default type parameters supply a fallback:

interface Result<T, E = Error> {
  ok: boolean;
  value?: T;
  error?: E;
}
type R = Result<User>;   // E defaults to Error

Useful for library APIs where a common case shouldn't require an explicit argument.

Two rules of thumb worth internalising

A type parameter used in exactly one place is usually doing nothing.

function log<T>(value: T): void {
  console.log(value);
}

T appears once, in one parameter, and nowhere else. It's not linking anything. This signature is identical in effect to log(value: unknown): void, and the generic version is worse because it looks like it means something. The value of a generic is in linking two positions — an input to a return, an object to its key, one parameter to another. If it doesn't link, delete it.

Generics do not exist at runtime. There is one first function in the emitted JavaScript. T is gone (Node 2). You cannot write new T(), cannot check if (T === String), cannot switch on the type argument. If you need construction, pass a constructor as a value:

function create<T>(Ctor: new () => T): T {
  return new Ctor();
}

The constructor is a runtime value, which is why this works and new T() doesn't.

When inference gets it wrong, and the tools for that

Three modern features exist for the cases where inference is technically correct and not what you wanted.

Widening losing your literals:

function pick<T>(options: T[]): T { return options[0]; }
const chosen = pick(["red", "green"]);   // string — literals lost

const type parameters, from TypeScript 5.0, fix it without the caller writing as const:

function pick<const T>(options: readonly T[]): T { return options[0]; }
const chosen = pick(["red", "green"]);   // "red" | "green"

Inference from the wrong argument:

function withDefault<T>(value: T | undefined, fallback: T): T {
  return value ?? fallback;
}
withDefault(maybeUser, {} as any);   // fallback pollutes T

NoInfer<T>, from 5.4, excludes a position from inference:

function withDefault<T>(value: T | undefined, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T {
  return value ?? fallback;
}

Now T is decided by value alone and fallback is merely checked against it.

Over-parameterisation. Three type parameters where one is always inferred as the same thing is a signature nobody can read. If you can't say the signature out loud, simplify: make a parameter concrete, or replace it with a union.

any poisoning generics

Worth naming explicitly because it's how type safety dies quietly:

const data: any = JSON.parse(raw);
const item = first(data);   // T infers as any — the result is any

Pass an any into a generic and the type parameter becomes any, and everything derived from it downstream is any too (Node 9). One untyped value at the top of a call chain can disable checking through several layers of perfectly well-written generic code.

In your project

Stage 3 of recast is where generics become unavoidable rather than optional. The registry holds a dozen converters, each with a different input format, output format, and options shape, all behind one dispatch function. Type the dispatcher non-generically and you have exactly the Java-1995 problem: every converter takes and returns a general type, and every call site casts. Type it generically — Converter<From, To, Options> with the relationship between the three constrained — and the dispatcher preserves what the caller actually has.

The options half is the interesting part and it's get<T, K extends keyof T> grown up: options keyed by conversion, derived from the registry, so selecting "JPEG at quality 80" gives you a quality number and selecting "split PDF" gives you a page range, with the compiler enforcing which controls the UI is allowed to render.

Stage 6's SDK is the same idea at the API boundary — one request<K extends keyof typeof routes> function where the body type and the response type are both computed from the route key, so there is no hand-written per-endpoint type anywhere in the codebase. The spec's warning that "generic inference through several layers fails in ways that produce errors pointing at the wrong place" is the honest one: when it breaks, over-annotate one link at a time until the error moves, which is the debugging technique nobody teaches explicitly.

Stage 7's extract<T>(schema: ZodType<T>, prompt: string): Promise<Result<T, ExtractionError>> ties three nodes together in a single signature — a generic (this node), constrained by a schema that exists at runtime (Node 15), returning a discriminated union (Node 4).

In qbank

Every Drizzle query in qbank is generic code doing exactly what this node describes. db.select().from(applications) returns a type computed from the table definition; add a .leftJoin() and the result type changes shape accordingly. That's a generic type parameterised by your schema, resolving per call site. The reason those editor tooltips are forty lines of nested generics is that you're seeing an instantiation rather than a declaration — and the working technique is to alias the result at the point of use (type AppWithCompany = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getAppWithCompany>>) rather than trying to read the raw inferred type.

Zod's z.infer<typeof schema> is the same mechanism from the other direction: a generic type extracting the static type from a runtime value, which is Node 15's central trick built on this node's machinery.

What an interviewer does with this

"What are generics and when would you use one?" — near-universal. Weak answers describe the syntax. Strong: "They make a type a parameter so reusable code preserves the caller's types instead of erasing them. The signal I need one is that two positions in a signature have to be linked — an argument to a return, or an object to one of its keys. If a type parameter appears only once, it isn't doing anything and I'd use unknown instead."

"Write a type-safe function that gets a property from an object." — a live-coding staple, and <T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] is the expected answer. Being able to explain each piece — keyof producing the key union, the constraint restricting K to real keys, indexed access computing the return — is what separates having memorised it from understanding it.

"Why can't you do new T() in a generic?" — tests whether erasure has landed. Generics are compile-time only; there's one function at runtime and T is gone. Mentioning that C# can do this because its generics are reified, while TypeScript's are erased like Java's, is the kind of detail that lands well.

"What does extends mean in a generic constraint?" — checks for a specific, common confusion. It means "is assignable to" — the structural relation — not class inheritance. Same keyword, unrelated meaning to class A extends B.

"You passed an object to a generic function and the inferred type is wider than you wanted. What are your options?" — a practical question that separates readers from users. Pass the type argument explicitly, use as const at the call site, use a const type parameter, or restructure the constraint so the inference site is narrower.

sections.title: Node 9 — The escape hatches
sections.content:
Where this sits

Every node so far built guarantees. This node is about the doors out of them — the constructs that let you tell the compiler to stop checking, or to trust you, or to admit it doesn't know. They exist because a type system with no escape hatch is a type system people abandon, and because external data genuinely arrives with no type at all. The skill here is not avoiding them; it's knowing precisely which ones keep checking on and which ones switch it off, because that distinction is most of what separates careful TypeScript from the other kind.

Every term, from absolute zero

Escape hatch — a deliberate opening in a system's rules, provided because the rules can't cover every real case. Not a bug or a workaround; a designed exit.

any — the type meaning "checking is off for this value." Every operation on it is permitted and yields any.

Top type — a type that every value belongs to. TypeScript has two: unknown (the safe one) and any (the unsafe one).

Bottom type — a type that no value belongs to. TypeScript's is never.

unknown — the safe top type, added in TypeScript 3.0 (July 2018). Accepts any value; permits nothing until you narrow.

never — the empty type. No value has it. It is assignable to everything, and nothing is assignable to it.

Assignable — from Node 2: usable where the target type is expected. The direction matters constantly in this node.

Type assertion — value as T, telling the compiler to treat a value as type T with no verification. Sometimes miscalled a "cast," which is wrong in an important way: a cast in C or Java may convert or check at runtime; a TypeScript assertion emits nothing.

Double assertion — value as unknown as T, used to force an assertion the compiler otherwise rejects as too far-fetched.

Non-null assertion — the postfix ! operator: x! claims x is neither null nor undefined, with no check.

Definite assignment assertion — the same ! in a declaration: let x!: string, meaning "something will assign this before it's read, trust me."

Type predicate — a function whose return type is written x is T, telling the compiler that a true return proves the argument is a T.

Assertion function — a function whose return type is written asserts x is T, narrowing for the remainder of the scope by throwing rather than returning false.

satisfies — an operator added in TypeScript 4.9 (November 2022) that checks a value against a type without replacing the value's inferred type.

Widening — from Node 1: the loss of literal precision when a value is assigned to something broader. satisfies exists specifically to avoid it.

Contagion / propagation — the way any spreads through everything it touches. Not a formal term, but it's the accurate description and worth naming.

The history — why each hatch exists

any and the adoption problem

any was in TypeScript from the beginning, and it exists for exactly one reason: the migration story from Node 0. If TypeScript could not represent "this value came from untyped JavaScript and I don't know what it is," then adopting it into an existing codebase would require typing everything before typing anything. any is the type of a value crossing from the untyped world into the typed one, and without it the gradual adoption that made TypeScript succeed would have been impossible.

It's also, straightforwardly, the biggest hole in the language. Both things are true, and the honest framing is that any bought adoption at the cost of safety, and the ecosystem has spent a decade adding tools to claw the safety back — noImplicitAny in the early days, unknown in 3.0, useUnknownInCatchVariables in 4.4.

unknown and the ten-year gap

For six years — 2012 to 2018 — there was no safe way to say "a value of any type." You wrote any and hoped. The pattern people wanted was obvious in hindsight: a top type that accepts everything but permits nothing, forcing a narrowing step before use.

unknown arrived in TypeScript 3.0, July 2018, and it is one of the cleanest features the language ever added, precisely because it changes nothing about existing code and gives you a strictly better default for new code. The gap is worth knowing about because it explains why so much existing code — including a great deal of library code and a great deal of what an LLM will suggest to you — uses any where unknown is now correct. It's not always carelessness; some of it is code written before the alternative existed.

never and the need for "impossible"

never has been there from early on, and it's the least intuitive of the three because its usefulness is indirect. It exists because a type system needs a way to say "no value can be here" — for a function that always throws, for a branch proven unreachable, for an intersection with no possible inhabitant. And once you have it, it becomes a tool: assigning to never is how you ask the compiler to prove exhaustiveness (Node 4).

satisfies and a fifteen-year annoyance

Before 4.9, you had two ways to relate a value to a type, and both lost something:

Annotate it (const x: Config = {...}) and the value gets checked but its type is replaced by the annotation — you lose the specific literal keys and values that the object actually has.

Assert it (const x = {...} as Config) and you keep... nothing useful, because the assertion switches off checking and also widens.

People wanted "check this against that type, and leave the inferred type alone." satisfies is exactly that, and it eliminated a large amount of code that had been reaching for as not to lie but simply to preserve precision.

The mechanism, traced

any: what it actually does, and why it spreads

const data: any = JSON.parse(raw);

data.foo.bar.baz();          // no error
data();                      // no error
data + 1;                    // no error
const n: number = data;      // no error

any is bidirectionally assignable — everything goes into it, and it goes into everything. Every property access succeeds and produces any. Every call succeeds and produces any. It is not "a type I don't know"; it is "stop checking here."

The contagion is the part that matters in practice, because it's how a single mistake becomes a codebase-wide loss of safety:

function parseConfig(raw: string): any {
  return JSON.parse(raw);
}

const config = parseConfig(text);     // any
const port = config.port;             // any
const url = `http://host:${port}`;    // string — the any stops here
const timeout = config.timeout * 2;   // any — and still spreading
setTimeout(handler, timeout);          // accepts any without complaint

Every value derived from an any is itself any unless something narrows it. Pass it into a generic (Node 8) and the type parameter becomes any, so the entire instantiation loses checking. Spread it into an object and the resulting properties soften. A single any at the top of a call chain can disable checking through several layers of otherwise-careful code, and nothing anywhere reports a problem, because reporting problems is precisely what you turned off.

This is why one any in a code review deserves more attention than a dozen other issues, and why noImplicitAny (Node 5) matters so much: without it, the compiler itself inserts any silently whenever it can't infer something.

unknown: the same acceptance, none of the permission

const data: unknown = JSON.parse(raw);

data.foo;         // error: 'data' is of type 'unknown'
data();           // error
const n: number = data;   // error: not assignable to 'number'

unknown accepts any value on the way in — assignment to it always works — and permits nothing on the way out. To use it, you must narrow it, using exactly the machinery from Node 4:

if (typeof data === "object" && data !== null && "port" in data) {
  // data: object & Record<"port", unknown>
}

That's deliberately tedious for a deeply nested shape, and the tedium is the correct signal: it's telling you that hand-narrowing arbitrary external data is the wrong tool, and a schema validator is the right one (Node 15). unknown doesn't solve the validation problem — it refuses to let you pretend you've solved it.

The rule to carry: anywhere you're tempted to write any for incoming data, unknown is the right answer. Parsed JSON, worker messages, caught errors, LLM output, third-party callbacks. The one legitimate remaining use for any is migration scaffolding — a deliberate, marked, temporary silencing of a file you intend to type properly.

never: the four places it appears

A function that never returns normally:

function fail(msg: string): never {
  throw new Error(msg);
}

Not void — void means "returns, with nothing useful." never means "does not return at all." The compiler uses this: code after a call to a never-returning function is understood to be unreachable, so narrowing carries through it the way it does after a throw.

A branch proven unreachable — the exhaustiveness pattern from Node 4:

default:
  const _exhaustive: never = e;

An impossible intersection (Node 3):

type Impossible = { a: string } & { a: number };   // a: never

The identity element of unions:

type T = string | never;   // just string

never disappears from unions, which looks like trivia and is structurally essential — it's exactly how Exclude<T, U> filters a union at Node 10. Members that match become never, and never vanishes, leaving the rest.

The assignability rule, which is the reverse of any and worth being able to state cleanly: never is assignable to everything; nothing is assignable to never. That makes sense once you read it as sets — the empty set is a subset of every set, and no non-empty set is a subset of the empty one.

Type assertions: the pure claim

const el = document.getElementById("root") as HTMLCanvasElement;

Nothing is checked, at compile time or runtime. Nothing is converted. The emitted JavaScript is document.getElementById("root") — the assertion vanished entirely (Node 2). If that element is actually a div, you have a compile-clean program that crashes the moment you call a canvas method.

Assertion is not conversion. value as number does not turn a string into a number; Number(value) does. This confuses people coming from languages where a cast may check or convert, and it's worth being explicit about because the mistake produces exactly the runtime failure the type system was meant to prevent.

TypeScript refuses assertions between sufficiently unrelated types:

const s = "hello";
const n = s as number;   // error: neither type sufficiently overlaps the other

Which produces the workaround, and the workaround is a warning sign in itself:

const n = s as unknown as number;   // compiles — and is a lie

as unknown as X means the compiler thought the assertion was implausible and you insisted. Occasionally justified when interfacing with badly-typed libraries; usually a signal that something upstream is modelled wrong.

The angle-bracket form <T>value is the older syntax and is unusable in .tsx files because it collides with JSX. Use as everywhere for consistency.

The non-null assertion, and why it's the most dangerous of all

const el = document.getElementById("root")!;
el.innerHTML = "";

! is an assertion that a value is neither null nor undefined. It's popular because it's short, and it's the single largest source of runtime null errors in codebases that have strictNullChecks on — which is an unfortunate irony worth stating plainly: every ! is a place where you enabled the null check and then individually overrode it.

Sometimes that's right — you can prove structurally that a map lookup succeeds because you just inserted the key. Often it's "I don't want to handle this right now," and the two look identical in the diff.

The habit worth building is that a ! should be accompanied by a reason you could say out loud. Where the reason is "it's in the HTML, it'll be there," the honest alternatives are a real check with a clear error, or the definite-assignment form if a framework guarantees initialisation:

class Service {
  private client!: Client;   // assigned in init(), not the constructor
  async init() { this.client = await connect(); }
}

That's the declaration form of ! — same trust, same risk, and it exists because strictPropertyInitialization (Node 5) would otherwise reject the field.

Type predicates: making the unsafe claim once, in one place

The safer relative of the assertion, and the thing you should reach for instead most of the time:

function isUser(value: unknown): value is User {
  return (
    typeof value === "object" &&
    value !== null &&
    "id" in value &&
    typeof (value as User).id === "string"
  );
}

if (isUser(data)) {
  data.id;   // narrowed to User
}

The return type value is User is the predicate. It tells the compiler: if this returns true, treat the argument as a User from here on. The compiler trusts it — it does not verify that your function actually checks anything, and a predicate returning true unconditionally is a silent lie.

So why is this better than an assertion, given that both are unverified claims? Because there is one of them. The claim lives in a single named function you can test, review, and fix, rather than being repeated as as User at forty call sites where nobody will ever revisit it. It's the same unsafe act, made auditable — which is a pattern worth naming generally, because it recurs: when you can't eliminate an unsafe operation, concentrate it.

Note the as User inside the predicate. That's the honest, contained use of an assertion: narrowing incrementally while building the proof.

Assertion functions are the throwing variant, added in TypeScript 3.7:
