function assertIsUser(value: unknown): asserts value is User {
  if (!isUser(value)) throw new Error("not a user");
}

assertIsUser(data);
data.id;   // narrowed for the rest of the scope

One quirk that catches everyone once: an assertion function must be called through an explicitly-typed reference — assigning it to a const without an annotation breaks the narrowing, because TypeScript requires the assertion signature to be statically known at the call site.

satisfies: check without widening

The problem it solves:

const config: Record<string, string> = {
  host: "localhost",
  port: "5432",
};
config.host;     // string
config.typo;     // string — no error, because Record<string, string> allows any key

The annotation checked the value and then replaced its type, so you lost the knowledge that exactly two keys exist.

const config = {
  host: "localhost",
  port: "5432",
} satisfies Record<string, string>;

config.host;     // string
config.typo;     // error: Property 'typo' does not exist

The value is checked against Record<string, string> — so a numeric value would be an error — and its inferred type is preserved, so the keys stay known.

The case where this really earns its place is a registry you want to derive types from:

const routes = {
  getUser: { method: "GET", path: "/users/:id" },
  createUser: { method: "POST", path: "/users" },
} satisfies Record<string, { method: string; path: string }>;

type RouteName = keyof typeof routes;   // "getUser" | "createUser"

With an annotation instead, keyof typeof routes would be string and useless. With as, nothing would be checked. satisfies gives you both, and it's why the modern idiom for typed configuration objects is satisfies rather than either of the older options.

It composes with as const (Node 7) — {...} as const satisfies Config gives you deep readonly literal types and validation, which is the pattern for a registry that both drives runtime behaviour and produces types.

The hierarchy, in one place

Worth holding as a single picture, because interviewers ask for exactly this comparison:

ConstructAcceptsPermitsChecking
anyeverythingeverythingoff
unknowneverythingnothing until narrowedon
nevernothing—on
x as T——off for that expression
x!——off for nullishness
x is T predicate——on, trusting one function
satisfies T——on, and preserves inference

In your project

Stage 2 of recast is where unknown and type predicates arrive together, and it's a genuinely good demonstration of why they belong together. A file's bytes arrive as raw data with no meaningful type; the detection function's job is to turn unknown into a DetectedFile discriminated union, and the only honest way to do that is a real check on the actual bytes. That's a type predicate whose body genuinely verifies — magic-byte comparison — rather than a predicate that asserts and hopes.

Stage 5's worker messages arrive as unknown from postMessage, which is the same boundary in a different transport, and the spec's instruction to type the protocol as a discriminated union and validate on receipt is precisely "don't reach for as here."

Stage 6's SDK will tempt you toward assertions constantly — the response body is any from res.json(), and as ResponseType compiles instantly. The spec's design of deriving the response type from the route registry exists so that you don't have to, and the discipline of noticing when you're about to write as is the actual lesson.

And Stage 10 plants four of its seven failures directly from this node: an any propagating from a WASM binding through three functions, an as on a worker message that's wrong because you changed one side of the protocol, a ! on a canvas context that genuinely is null when the canvas is too large, and an out-of-range index typed as present. Each one compiles cleanly. That's the point.

In qbank

Two specific things worth grepping for in qbank, because both are near-certain to be there and both are this node.

Every catch block: if it reads error.message without narrowing, that's either useUnknownInCatchVariables being off or an assertion silencing it, and it's the pattern where an error handler throws its own error while handling an error — producing a stack trace that points at your logging code instead of the actual failure.

Every place the Anthropic API's tool-call arguments are read. They arrive as JSON, which means any unless something stopped it, and an annotation or an as there is the exact "compiles clean, wrong at runtime" shape this node describes. Whatever you find, that's the honest before-picture for the Node 15 rebuild.

What an interviewer does with this

"What's the difference between any and unknown?" — one of the most reliable screening questions in TypeScript interviews, because it cleanly separates people who have thought about the type system from people who have used it. Strong: "Both accept any value. any switches checking off and propagates — pass it into a generic and the whole instantiation loses safety. unknown keeps checking on and forces narrowing before use. Anywhere external data enters, unknown is correct, and any is really only justified as migration scaffolding."

"What is never and where have you actually used it?" — the second half matters more than the first. The exhaustiveness pattern is the answer that shows real use: assigning a narrowed value to never in a default branch so that adding a union member becomes a compile error at every site that must change.

"Is a type assertion the same as a cast?" — a small trap. No: nothing is converted, nothing is checked, and the assertion emits no code at all. as number does not parse a string.

"When would you use satisfies over an annotation?" — increasingly common as a "how current are you" question. When you need the value checked but want to keep its precise inferred type — a config or registry object you'll derive a union from with keyof typeof.

"How do you safely handle a value whose type you don't know?" — the answer chains this node into Node 15: type it unknown, then either narrow with a type predicate that genuinely checks, or — for anything with real structure — parse it with a schema and derive the type from the schema rather than asserting.

"What's wrong with !?" — nothing, sometimes, and that's the answer to give: it's a valid tool where you can prove non-nullness structurally, and it's the largest source of runtime null errors in strict codebases because it's usually used where the reason is "I don't want to handle this." Each one should come with a reason you could say out loud.

sections.title: Node 10 — Type-level programming
sections.content:
Where this sits

Node 8 gave you types with parameters. This node discovers that those parameters can be computed with — that TypeScript's type layer is itself a small programming language, in which you write programs whose inputs are types and whose outputs are types. It's the heaviest node in the topic, it's what makes libraries like Zod and Drizzle possible, and it's where a codebase most easily becomes unmaintainable if you enjoy it too much.

Every term, from absolute zero

Type space and value space — two separate worlds in a TypeScript file. Value space is ordinary JavaScript: variables, functions, actual data. Type space is everything after a colon, inside angle brackets, or in a type/interface declaration. They are genuinely separate — a name can exist in both and mean different things — and confusing the two is the most common early stumble in this node.

keyof — an operator in type space producing the union of a type's keys.

typeof (in type space) — an operator lifting a value's type into type space. Spelled identically to JavaScript's runtime typeof from Node 2, and completely unrelated to it. Context determines which one you're using.

Indexed access type — reading the type at a key: T["name"]. Written like a property access, but performed on types.

Mapped type — a type built by transforming every member of another type: { [K in keyof T]: ... }.

Key remapping — renaming keys during a mapped type, using as inside the mapping.

Modifier — ? (optional) and readonly, which mapped types can add or remove. -? removes optionality; -readonly removes immutability.

Conditional type — a branch in type space: T extends U ? X : Y. Again extends means assignable to (Node 2), not inheritance.

Distribution — the behaviour where a conditional type applied to a naked type parameter is evaluated separately for each member of a union, and the results re-unioned.

Naked type parameter — a type parameter appearing on its own on the left of extends in a conditional, not wrapped in anything. T extends U is naked; [T] extends [U] is not.

infer — a keyword declaring a type variable to be captured by pattern-matching inside a conditional type.

Template literal type — a type built from string patterns, using backticks: ` on${Capitalize<K>} `. Added in TypeScript 4.1.

Recursive type — a type defined partly in terms of itself, used for walking nested structures or strings character by character.

Instantiation depth — how many nested type expansions the compiler performs. There's a hard limit, and hitting it is a specific error message.

Utility type — one of the type transformations shipped in TypeScript's standard library: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record and friends. All are written in TypeScript itself.

Branded type / nominal simulation — introduced at Node 2; built properly here, since it needs intersection plus a phantom member.

Homomorphic mapped type — a mapped type of the exact form { [K in keyof T]: ... } over a generic T. The term matters because these preserve modifiers and array/tuple structure automatically, while other mapped types don't. "Homomorphic" is borrowed from mathematics and means, loosely, structure-preserving.

The history — why a type system became a programming language

This was not planned. TypeScript's type system acquired computational power incrementally, each feature added to solve a specific practical problem, and the result is more powerful than anyone designed.

Mapped types and keyof arrived in TypeScript 2.1, December 2016. The motivating problem was concrete and boring: people were hand-writing "the same interface but with everything optional" over and over for update payloads and configuration objects, and those hand-written copies drifted from the original. Partial<T> made the transformation expressible once. Pick, Readonly and Record shipped in the same release.

Conditional types and infer arrived in TypeScript 2.8, March 2018. The motivation was again specific: expressing things like "the type a promise resolves to" or "a function's return type" required the type system to inspect a type and branch on its shape, which nothing before could do.

Template literal types arrived in 4.1, November 2020, driven by real library needs — typing event names like onClick derived from click, and typing route parameters extracted from a path string.

At each step the goal was to remove duplication in ordinary code. The consequence, which fell out rather than being intended, is that the type layer is Turing-complete: people have implemented arithmetic, sorting algorithms, and even a chess engine in TypeScript types. That's a curiosity rather than a recommendation, and it's worth knowing chiefly as evidence for the discipline this node ends with — the language is powerful enough to let you build something nobody on your team can maintain.

The genuinely important consequence is more mundane and more valuable: the same computation that removes duplication between two types also lets a library derive an entire API from your data. That's why Zod can turn a schema value into a static type, why Drizzle can turn a table definition into a row type, and why a route registry can type an entire SDK. Every one of those is this node doing real work.

The mechanism, traced

keyof: the union of keys

interface User { id: string; name: string; age: number }

type UserKey = keyof User;   // "id" | "name" | "age"

keyof produces a union of literal types (Node 4) — the keys as string literals. That immediately connects to everything unions can do: you can narrow it, constrain a generic to it (Node 8's K extends keyof T), and exclude members from it.

Two edge behaviours worth knowing. keyof on a type with an index signature (Node 3) gives you string | number rather than specific keys, because that's genuinely what the type says. And keyof on an array or tuple includes all the array methods and the numeric indices, which is why you use T[number] rather than keyof T to get element types.

typeof in type space: lifting a value into types

const config = {
  host: "localhost",
  port: 5432,
};

type Config = typeof config;   // { host: string; port: number }

This is the bridge between the two worlds, and the direction matters: it goes from value space to type space, never the reverse. You can ask "what is the type of this value?" You cannot ask "give me a value of this type," because types don't exist at runtime (Node 2).

Combined with as const from Node 7, it's how you derive types from real data:

const STATUSES = ["pending", "active", "done"] as const;
type Status = typeof STATUSES[number];   // "pending" | "active" | "done"

Walk that right-hand side once more, since it's the single most useful two-operator combination in the language. typeof STATUSES gives the type readonly ["pending", "active", "done"]. Indexing it with number asks "what type is at any numeric position?" — which for a tuple is the union of everything in it.

Indexed access: reading a type at a key

type Name = User["name"];              // string
type IdOrAge = User["id" | "age"];     // string | number
type AllValues = User[keyof User];     // string | number

Indexing with a union of keys gives a union of the corresponding types. That last line — T[keyof T] — is the general "union of all value types" idiom, and it's how you go from an object to the set of things it can contain.

Mapped types: transforming every member

type Optional<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };

type PartialUser = Optional<User>;
// { id?: string; name?: string; age?: number }

Read [K in keyof T] as a loop in type space: for each key K in the union keyof T, produce a member. The value type is T[K] — indexed access, per key. This is Partial<T>, and it's genuinely how Partial is defined in TypeScript's standard library.

Modifiers are added or removed with + and -:

type Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };      // removes optionality
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }; // removes readonly

-? is not punctuation soup once you know it's "minus optional."

Key remapping with as renames keys during mapping:

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K]
};

type UserGetters = Getters<User>;
// { getId: () => string; getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }

And mapping a key to never removes it, which is how filtering works:

type OnlyStrings<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K]
};

type S = OnlyStrings<User>;   // { id: string; name: string }

The age key mapped to never and vanished — the same "never disappears" behaviour from Node 9, applied to keys.

The utility types, and writing them yourself

Every one of these is a few lines of the above. Being able to reconstruct them is a common screening exercise, and more usefully it proves the machinery isn't magic:

type Partial<T>    = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type Required<T>   = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type Readonly<T>   = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type Record<K extends keyof any, V> = { [P in K]: V };

Omit is the interesting one, because it's built from two others:

type Omit<T, K> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;

Which requires Exclude, which requires conditionals and distribution — so it's the natural bridge to the next section.

The rest worth knowing by name: ReturnType<F>, Parameters<F>, Awaited<T> (unwraps promises, including nested ones), NonNullable<T> (removes null and undefined), Extract<T, U> (keeps matching union members), and InstanceType<C>.

Conditional types: branching in type space

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";

type A = IsString<"hello">;   // "yes"
type B = IsString<42>;        // "no"

extends here is assignability, as always. The syntax is deliberately the ternary operator from JavaScript, one level up.

Real use looks like this:

type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;

type X = Unwrap<Promise<string>>;   // string
type Y = Unwrap<number>;            // number

infer U is the pattern-matching part, and it's the piece that makes conditionals powerful rather than merely selective. It says: "if T matches the shape Promise<something>, bind that something to U and let me use it in the true branch." The compiler performs structural matching and reads off the binding — the same mechanism as generic inference from Node 8, applied inside a type expression.

infer is how the standard library's inspection utilities are written:

type ReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type Parameters<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;

Parameters captures the whole parameter list as a tuple (Node 7), which is why the result is [string, number] rather than a union.

Distribution: the behaviour that surprises everyone once

type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;

type R = ToArray<string | number>;
// Expected: (string | number)[]
// Actual:   string[] | number[]

Here's what happened, precisely. T is a naked type parameter on the left of extends, and the argument is a union. In that specific situation, TypeScript evaluates the conditional once per union member and unions the results. So ToArray<string | number> becomes ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>, which is string[] | number[].

This is not a quirk to route around — it's the mechanism that makes union filtering work at all:

type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;

type Status = "pending" | "active" | "done";
type NotDone = Exclude<Status, "done">;   // "pending" | "active"

Distribution evaluates the conditional for each member: "pending" doesn't extend "done" so it stays; "active" stays; "done" does extend "done" so it becomes never — and never vanishes from unions (Node 9). Three lines of type code, and you have union subtraction.

To suppress distribution, wrap both sides in tuples so the parameter isn't naked:

type ToArrayNonDist<T> = [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never;
type R2 = ToArrayNonDist<string | number>;   // (string | number)[]

You'll need this the first time you want to test a union as a whole rather than member by member — for example, checking whether a type is exactly never, which requires the non-distributive form because distributing over never (a union with zero members) produces never immediately.

Template literal types: strings, computed

type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`;
type Click = EventName<"click">;   // "onClick"

Capitalize is one of four built-in intrinsic string types — with Uppercase, Lowercase and Uncapitalize — implemented inside the compiler rather than in TypeScript, because character manipulation isn't otherwise expressible.

Combined with unions, template literals multiply out:

type Size = "sm" | "lg";
type Colour = "red" | "blue";
type Class = `${Colour}-${Size}`;
// "red-sm" | "red-lg" | "blue-sm" | "blue-lg"

Note that this is a combinatorial expansion — two unions of ten members each produce a hundred literal types, and three produce a thousand. That's the first honest hint of Node 18: template literal types over large unions are one of the reliable ways to make a compile slow.

And with infer, they can parse:

type PathParams<T extends string> =
  T extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param]: string } & PathParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : T extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : {};

type P = PathParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// { userId: string } & { postId: string }

This is recursion, pattern matching, and mapped types together, and it's exactly the utility recast Stage 6 needs. It's also the point at which you should feel slightly uncomfortable — which is the correct response, and the subject of the next section.

Branded types, built properly

Node 2 established the problem: UserId and PostId are both string, so structural typing makes them interchangeable. The fix uses intersection (Node 3) with a member that exists only in type space:

declare const brand: unique symbol;

type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [brand]: B };

type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type PostId = Brand<string, "PostId">;

function makeUserId(s: string): UserId {
  return s as UserId;   // the one contained lie
}

const uid = makeUserId("u_1");
const pid: PostId = uid;   // error — brands differ

unique symbol makes the brand key impossible to produce accidentally elsewhere. At runtime the property doesn't exist — the emitted code is just a string — so the entire safety mechanism is a compile-time fiction, deliberately. The as inside the constructor is the single place the fiction is asserted, which is the Node 9 pattern of concentrating an unsafe act into one auditable location.

Recursion, and the limit

type DeepPartial<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]?: T[K] extends object ? DeepPartial<T[K]> : T[K]
};

Recursion works, and TypeScript 4.1 raised the limits substantially (tail-recursive conditional types can now handle roughly a thousand iterations). But there is a hard cap, and hitting it produces:

> Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.

Read that error as "stop", not as "optimise." It almost always means the type is doing something better done at runtime, or that the recursion lacks a proper base case.

The discipline

This node's real content isn't the operators — it's knowing when not to use them.

Use the built-in utilities freely. Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType are universally understood and cost nothing in comprehension.

Write a simple mapped or conditional type when it removes real duplication. If two types must stay in lockstep and someone will eventually forget, compute one from the other.

Treat anything needing a comment to explain as a design smell. Not forbidden — flagged. A clever type is written once and read fifty times, usually by someone with less context than you had.

A type is worth what it prevents. A recursive conditional catching a bug nobody would write, at the cost of a slow build and an error message nobody can parse, is a net loss. That's Node 18's judgement arriving early, and it's a better interview answer than any amount of type-level virtuosity — because "I know when to stop" is what an interviewer actually wants to hear from someone who clearly can do this.

In your project

Stage 4 of recast is this node, deployed on a genuine problem. The conversion registry is a graph — HEIC to JPEG exists, JPEG to PDF exists — and the question "is there a route from HEIC to EPUB?" is answered by walking the edges. Both at runtime, with an ordinary breadth-first search, and at compile time, with a recursive conditional type over the as const edge list, so that convert(file, "heic", "epub") fails to compile if no route exists.

That single feature uses as const (Node 7) to get the edges into type space, typeof to lift them, indexed access to read them, conditional types with infer to match a step, distribution to consider every candidate edge, and recursion to chain steps into a route. It is the whole node in one utility — and it's a rare case where the type-level version is genuinely the simplest correct design, because the alternative is hand-maintaining a table of every valid pair as the format list grows.

The spec's two disciplines for that stage are both from this node's ending. Cap the recursion depth explicitly, so a mistake produces a clear failure rather than the excessively-deep error. And keep the type-level and runtime pathfinders adjacent with a test asserting they agree, because two implementations of one idea is exactly the drift this node exists to eliminate.

Stage 6's path-parameter type is the PathParams utility above, applied to real routes. Stage 8's branded IDs are the branding pattern. And Stage 3's options-keyed-by-conversion is a mapped type over the registry — which means adding a format to one as const object updates the format union, the options types, the UI's controls, and the API schemas, with nothing else edited. That's the payoff sentence for the whole node.

In qbank

Both major libraries in qbank are built entirely on this node, and reading them with these operators in hand is the fastest way to stop finding them opaque.

z.infer<typeof schema> is a conditional type with infer extracting the output type from a Zod schema object — so when you write a schema as a value and get a type out, what's happening is typeof lifting the value into type space and a conditional pattern-matching its internal type parameter. Nothing mystical.

Drizzle's typeof applications.$inferSelect is the same shape: a table object whose type carries the column definitions, and a mapped type turning those columns into a row shape. The forty-line editor tooltips you get from a join are an instantiation being displayed, not a declaration — and the practical technique is naming the result with a type alias at the point of use rather than trying to read the raw expansion.

What an interviewer does with this

"Implement Pick and Omit yourself." — a common screening exercise, precisely because it proves the utilities aren't compiler magic. Pick is a mapped type over a constrained key union; Omit is Pick over Exclude<keyof T, K>, which forces you to explain distribution as well.

"What does infer do?" — strong answers give both the definition and a use: it binds a type variable by structural pattern-matching inside a conditional, and it's how ReturnType, Parameters and Awaited are implemented.

"Why did my conditional type produce a union instead of what I expected?" — the distribution question. A naked type parameter distributes over unions; wrap it in a tuple to stop. Being able to say why distribution is desirable — it's what makes Exclude work — shows you understand it as a feature rather than a trap.

"How would you make two string ID types incompatible?" — branded types: intersect with a phantom property, construct through a single function that performs the one assertion, note that it's entirely compile-time and there's no runtime enforcement.

"When is type-level programming a bad idea?" — increasingly asked, and the best question on this list. When it needs a comment to explain, when its error message is unreadable, when it measurably slows the build, or when a runtime check would catch the same bug for a fraction of the cost. A candidate who can do this and says that unprompted reads as senior; one who only demonstrates cleverness reads as a future maintenance problem.

sections.title: Node 11 — Classes and enums
sections.content:
Where this sits

Every node so far has described things that vanish at compile time. This node is the exception: classes are real runtime objects, and TypeScript's class layer adds features that are not purely erasable. That makes this a different category from everything before it, and it's why the constructs here are the ones causing friction as the ecosystem moves toward runtimes that strip types (Node 19).

Every term, from absolute zero

Class — a template for creating objects with shared structure and behaviour. JavaScript gained class syntax in ES2015 (2015); before that, the same thing was done directly with functions and prototypes (Node 2).

Instance — an object created from a class with new.

Constructor — the function that runs when an instance is created, setting up its initial state.

Field / property — a value stored on an instance. Method — a function stored on the class, shared by all instances via the prototype.

Access modifier — a keyword controlling who may read or write a member: public, private, protected. TypeScript-only, and compile-time only.

#private field — JavaScript's own private field syntax, standardised in ES2022, genuinely inaccessible from outside the class at runtime.

Parameter property — TypeScript shorthand declaring and assigning a field directly in the constructor signature: constructor(private name: string).

abstract — a class that cannot be instantiated directly, and members subclasses must implement.

implements — a declaration that a class satisfies an interface. Checked structurally (Node 2); creates no nominal relationship.

Enum — a TypeScript construct naming a set of related constants. Unlike everything else in this topic, it emits a runtime object.

Numeric enum / string enum — enums whose members have number values (the default) or explicit string values.

Reverse mapping — a numeric enum's emitted object maps both name→value and value→name, so Status[0] gives back "Active".

Namespace — TypeScript's pre-ES-modules way of grouping declarations. Legacy; also emits runtime code.

Decorator — an annotation attached to a class or member with @, which can observe or modify it: @Injectable(), @Column().

emitDecoratorMetadata — a compiler option that writes type information into the output for decorated members. Introduced at Node 2 as the one place TypeScript deliberately leaks types into runtime.

Erasable syntax — syntax that can be removed by simply deleting characters, with no rewriting. Everything in TypeScript is erasable except the constructs in this node.

The mechanism, traced

Access modifiers are annotations, not walls

class Account {
  private balance = 1000;
  getBalance() { return this.balance; }
}

const a = new Account();
a.balance;                    // error: Property 'balance' is private
(a as any).balance;           // 1000 — no error, works fine
console.log(JSON.stringify(a)); // {"balance":1000}

private is enforced by the compiler and by nothing else. The emitted JavaScript is a plain field. Anyone can read it at runtime with a cast (Node 9), it appears in serialisation, and it's visible in a debugger. This is not a bug — it's erasure (Node 2) applied consistently — but it means private communicates intent to other developers, not a security or encapsulation boundary.

JavaScript's own #private is the real thing:

class Account {
  #balance = 1000;
  getBalance() { return this.#balance; }
}

const a = new Account();
(a as any).balance;             // undefined
JSON.stringify(a);              // {} — genuinely hidden

#balance is enforced by the JavaScript engine itself. It's absent from serialisation and inaccessible from outside the class body at runtime. The two coexist, mean genuinely different things, and the choice is real: private for ordinary code organisation, # when hiding actually matters.

One quirk worth knowing from Node 2: classes with private or protected members compare nominally, not structurally. Two classes with identical shapes, each declaring private id: string, are not assignable to each other — because the compiler tracks which declaration the private member came from. It's the one corner of TypeScript that behaves like Java, and it occasionally explains an error message that otherwise looks impossible.

Parameter properties: the first non-erasable thing

class Service {
  constructor(private client: Client, public name: string) {}
}

This declares two fields and assigns them from the constructor arguments, in one stroke. The emitted JavaScript is:

class Service {
  constructor(client, name) {
    this.client = client;
    this.name = name;
  }
}

Notice what happened: the compiler generated assignments that weren't in your source. This isn't deletion — it's code generation. Which means a tool that only strips types (Node 14, Node 19) cannot handle this syntax, because there's nothing to strip; there's something to add. That's the first crack in the "TypeScript is purely erased" story, and it's why this construct appears in the erasableSyntaxOnly prohibition list.

It's also the syntax that makes NestJS-style dependency injection concise, which is why it's common in backend codebases despite the erasability problem.

implements is structural, not a promise

interface Logger { log(msg: string): void }

class ConsoleLogger implements Logger {
  log(msg: string) { console.log(msg); }
}

class SilentLogger {           // no `implements` clause
  log(msg: string) {}
}

const l: Logger = new SilentLogger();   // fine — structurally compatible

implements asks the compiler to check that this class satisfies the interface, which is useful — you find out at the class declaration rather than at some distant use site. But it creates no exclusive relationship: any structurally compatible class is equally assignable (Node 2). It's a check, not a claim of membership.

Enums: the odd feature out

enum Status {
  Active,
  Cancelled,
}

Every other type-level construct in this topic disappears at compile time. This one emits:

var Status;
(function (Status) {
  Status[Status["Active"] = 0] = "Active";
  Status[Status["Cancelled"] = 1] = "Cancelled";
})(Status || (Status = {}));

A real object, in your bundle, at runtime. The nested assignment is the reverse mapping: Status.Active is 0, and Status[0] is "Active". That's occasionally useful and mostly surprising — it means iterating the object's keys gives you both names and numbers.

The soundness problem is worse than the size:

function setStatus(s: Status) {}
setStatus(47);   // no error in many TypeScript versions/positions

For historical reasons, arbitrary numbers have been assignable to numeric enum types in various positions — so a value that is not a member of the enum passes the check. TypeScript has tightened this over time and it varies by version and context, which is itself a reason to be wary: a construct whose safety depends on which compiler version you're on is a construct to avoid.

String enums avoid the numeric hole and the reverse mapping:

enum Status {
  Active = "active",
  Cancelled = "cancelled",
}

Better, but still emits an object and still isn't erasable.

The modern alternative, which is what the rest of this topic has been building toward:

const STATUS = {
  Active: "active",
  Cancelled: "cancelled",
} as const;

type Status = typeof STATUS[keyof typeof STATUS];   // "active" | "cancelled"

That's Node 7's as const plus Node 10's typeof and indexed access. You get a runtime object to iterate when you want one, a literal union that narrows naturally (Node 4), no reverse mapping, no unsoundness, and fully erasable syntax. The only thing you lose is the enum keyword.

So the honest position: enums are defensible where you genuinely need a runtime object and the ergonomics of enum syntax, and a string-literal union is the better default everywhere else. The argument is no longer stylistic — it's compatibility with where the ecosystem is going.

Namespaces: legacy, and also emitting

namespace Utils {
  export function parse(s: string) { return s.trim(); }
}

This predates ES modules and solved the same problem — grouping declarations, avoiding global name collisions — before JavaScript had a module system. It emits an object, same as an enum. You will meet namespaces in old code and in declaration files (Node 12), where they're still used to structure ambient declarations. You should not write new ones; use ES modules.

Decorators, and which flavour you're on

@Injectable()
class UserService {
  @Column({ type: "varchar" })
  name: string;
}

Decorators are functions that receive the thing they decorate and can observe or modify it. They're how Angular, NestJS and TypeORM work — dependency injection, ORM column mapping, route registration.

The version confusion is real and worth being precise about. TypeScript had an experimental implementation behind experimentalDecorators for roughly a decade, tracking an early TC39 proposal. TypeScript 5.0 (March 2023) shipped the standardised ECMAScript decorators, which have different semantics and are not fully compatible with the experimental ones. Frameworks built on the old behaviour still require experimentalDecorators: true. So the practical question when you open a decorated codebase is: which flag is set, and therefore which decorator semantics apply.

emitDecoratorMetadata is the deeper oddity. With it on, the compiler writes runtime metadata about types — a design:type record readable via the reflect-metadata library. That's the one place TypeScript deliberately violates erasure, and it's what lets NestJS infer what to inject from a constructor parameter's type alone. Useful, and a genuine exception to everything Node 2 said.

When classes are actually right

Given that most data modelling in TypeScript is better served by plain object types and discriminated unions (Node 4), it's worth naming where classes genuinely earn their place.

Error hierarchies, because instanceof narrowing works and because extending Error gives you stack traces:

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, readonly code: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "AppError";
  }
}
class NotFoundError extends AppError {}

With the caveat from Node 2 that instanceof dies across serialisation boundaries — so an error crossing a worker, queue or HTTP response needs a literal discriminant property to survive.

Framework-mandated structures, where NestJS or TypeORM require classes and there's no argument to have.

Stateful objects with genuine behaviour — a connection pool, a cache, a parser holding position — where methods operating on private state is the natural model.

In your project

Stage 6 of recast builds the error hierarchy: a base ConversionError with subclasses for the distinct failure modes, plus a type predicate to recognise them (Node 9) and one handler mapping them to HTTP status codes. The spec's note about errors crossing the queue boundary is this node meeting Node 2 — a NotFoundError serialised into BullMQ and back is a plain object, so the class-based check silently stops working and a kind discriminant is what survives.

Stage 10 plants a numeric enum for compression level and feeds it a number that isn't a member, which compiles and produces nonsense downstream. Stage 11 then removes it: turning on erasableSyntaxOnly to run the CLI under Node's native type stripping breaks on that enum, on any parameter property, and on any namespace — and the fix is exactly the as const object plus literal union above. That's where this node's argument stops being theoretical and becomes a build error you have to resolve.

In qbank

Worth checking directly: whether qbank uses enums anywhere, and whether its Fastify plugin classes or error types use parameter properties. Both are common in generated or LLM-suggested TypeScript, and both are the specific constructs that would block that codebase from ever running under type stripping. It's a small, concrete modernisation you could make and explain — which is more valuable in an interview than a larger change you can't justify.

What an interviewer does with this

"Is private in TypeScript actually private?" — a quick separator. No: compile-time only, readable at runtime, visible in JSON.stringify. JavaScript's #private is the enforced one. Volunteering that classes with private members compare nominally rather than structurally is a strong extra.

"Should you use enums?" — increasingly common, and the good answer is now about erasability rather than taste. Enums emit a runtime object, numeric ones have an assignability hole, and they break under erasableSyntaxOnly — so they're incompatible with runtimes that strip types. A string-literal union derived from an as const object gives the same closed set with narrowing, no emit, and no unsoundness.

"What's the state of decorators in TypeScript?" — tests currency. Experimental implementation for a decade behind experimentalDecorators; standard ECMAScript decorators shipped in 5.0; the two aren't fully compatible, so frameworks like NestJS and TypeORM still pin to the experimental flag. emitDecoratorMetadata is the one place TypeScript writes type information into the runtime.

"When would you use a class rather than an interface and a plain object?" — error hierarchies where instanceof helps, framework requirements, and objects with genuine private state and behaviour. Noting that most application data is better modelled as discriminated unions shows you're not reaching for classes by default out of habit from another language.
